accuracy.evidence: Matches the Year 6 Ratio and proportion statements in the English national curriculum (relative sizes of two quantities, percentages for comparison, unequal sharing, scale factors) and the Year 5 per cent, fraction and decimal link. Every number was checked: 3 : 2 is 3 out of 5, 60%, 3/5 and 0.6; 6 : 4 is equivalent to 3 : 2; 1 out of 4 blue is the ratio 1 : 3; twice as much yellow is 1 : 2, so yellow is 2 out of 3.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets reading 2 : 3 as the fraction 2/3 (step 1 trap at 1 : 4 and mastery m2), parts in the wrong order (step 0 trap at 2 : 3), additive scaling 3 : 2 to 6 : 5 (step 3 prediction plus a visibly different pot colour), and joining digits so 3 out of 5 becomes 35% (step 2 trap on the grid and challenge reply). The adult notes name each slip.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagratio is a paint-mixing bench: two draggable rows of cups feed a pot whose colour comes from the yellow share, a target pot to match for equivalent ratios, and a hundred grid you drag to shade for per cent. It passes the 30% shingle gate and differs from the fraction labs (bars and number lines) and the percentage change lab (multipliers).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step uses the same cups to change one idea: build part-to-part 3 : 2, then rebuild so blue is 1 out of 4 of the whole, then convert 3 out of 5 to 60 out of 100 beside a five-block bar, then match the 3 : 2 colour using scale factor 2, then build the relative-size sentence 'twice as much yellow' at 9 cups. The live text names the ratio and the proportion after every change.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions come before the action: how to write 3 : 2, what proportion is blue, 3 out of 5 as a per cent, whether 6 : 5 matches 3 : 2 and what proportion is yellow at 1 : 2. Each wrong option is a known slip (3 : 5, 2 : 3, 35%, additive scaling, 1 out of 2) and the reveal line quotes the learner's guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions map each wrong option to a targeted why() reply, such as 'That compares part with part. A proportion is out of the whole, so add the parts first', 'Per cent means out of 100, not the digits side by side', 'Adding the same amount changes the ratio. Multiply instead' and the 'for every' and colon cue for a ratio.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences about cups of paint, say each ratio aloud ('3 to 2') and pass the learner kid FK gate. Adult paragraphs quote the curriculum, list the precise vocabulary (part-to-part, part-to-whole, scale factor, relative size, unequal) and name the common mistakes, and pass the learner adult gate.

no_filler.evidence: No stock phrases: each sentence defines a word, works a number or names a slip. The family tip uses squash and water, a real mix at home, and asks the three lesson questions in order: the ratio, the proportion out of the whole jug, the per cent, then how to scale it up and keep the taste.

mobile.evidence: Walked through on iPhone 13 in dark and light themes: the two cup rows, the pot and both text lines fit the canvas width, the hundred grid sits beside the 3 out of 5 bar with readable labels, and the plus and minus buttons wrap onto rows under the canvas with large tap targets.

accessibility.evidence: axe reports no violations in light and dark themes. Every drag has a button twin (+ blue, − blue, +10, +1 and so on, each with an aria-label), the canvas aria-label and the live text state the ratio and proportion in words, so colour is never the only cue, and challenge feedback is in a polite live region.
